meanings: links a modifier to a noun

components.note: 白 (white, bright) — an early meaning of 的 was 'bright, clear', as in 的确 'truly'
勺 (sháo) is the sound part, only a loose match for de today

example.fact: 的 is the most frequent character in written Chinese. It links a modifier to a noun (我的书 'my book'), and it can also stand in for the noun itself: 我的 means 'mine'. In the 是…的 pattern it stresses details such as when or how something happened.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — the modern form shows a hand-like element on the left
戈 (spear, halberd) — a weapon on the right; the pairing looks like a hand holding a weapon, a memory aid rather than the proven origin

example.fact: Add 们 to make 我们 'we'. 我们 can include the listener, while 咱们 explicitly does (mainly in northern speech). Chinese often drops 我 when the subject is obvious, so a bare 想去 can already mean 'I want to go'.

components.note: 亻 (person) — the pronoun refers to a person
尔 (ěr) — an old second-person word that 你 grew out of

example.fact: 你 is the informal 'you'; the polite form is 您 (nín), which adds 心 'heart' below. Use 您 for elders, customers and strangers of higher status. Plural is 你们, and written Chinese uses 你 for both men and women.

components.note: 日 (sun) — the upper part; the story is that the sun is the clearest 'right' thing, a mnemonic more than proven origin
疋 (foot/ 'straight' shape) — the lower part of the character

example.fact: 是 links nouns (我是学生) but is NOT used before most adjectives: say 他很高, not 他是高. Answering yes/no questions, Chinese echoes the verb: 你是学生吗？— 是 means 'yes'.

components.note: A small hooked stroke; the character originally meant 'to finish', which is how the particle grew a 'completed' sense

example.fact: 了 marks a completed action after a verb (吃了) or a new situation at the end of a sentence (下雨了 'it's raining now'). It is not simply a past tense: 明天我吃了饭就去 uses it for a future completed step. Read as liǎo it means 'to finish', as in 了解.

components.note: Origin is debated; the abstract shape is simply learned as the negation word used before verbs and adjectives

example.fact: 不 turns into bú before a fourth-tone syllable: bú shì, bú qù. It negates present and future (我不去) while 没 negates 'have' and past events (我没去). The tone change is shown in pinyin but the character stays the same.

components.note: 土 (earth) — being 'at' a place on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound; zài is a near match

example.fact: 在 works three ways: as a verb ('to be located', 他在家), as a preposition before a place (在北京工作), and as a progressive marker before a verb (我在吃饭 'I'm eating'). Put 在+place BEFORE the verb, unlike English.

components.note: 亻 (person) — a pronoun for a person
也 (yě) is the sound hint; the match is weak in modern Mandarin

example.fact: 他, 她 and 它 sound identical (tā) and differ only in writing, so spoken Chinese has no he/she distinction. 他 historically served as a generic 'other (person)', and 他们 is still used for mixed or unspecified groups.

components.note: 女 (woman) — the left part
子 (child) — the right part; a woman with a child, a traditional picture of something good

example.english: The weather is very good today.
example.fact: 好 can sit before a verb to mean 'easy to': 好吃 'tasty', 好看 'nice-looking'. Spoken as 好 on its own it means 'OK'. It is also read hào ('to like') in words like 爱好, a different reading.

components.note: 月 here is the 肉 'meat' shape rather than the moon — the usual account is a hand holding a piece of meat, i.e., possession

example.fact: 有 is negated with 没, never 不: 我没有钱 'I have no money'. It also means 'there is': 桌子上有一本书. In Cantonese the same idea uses 冇 for 'not have', a character built from 有 by removing two strokes.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — a motion radical; the traditional form 這 also had it
文 is the simplified stand-in for the traditional right-hand part, so it is a shorthand rather than a meaning clue

example.fact: In speech 这 is often said zhèi, especially before a measure word (这个 zhèige). Before a number or measure word, use 这 + measure + noun: 这本书. Its partner is 那 (nà) 'that', and 这儿/这里 means 'here'.

components.note: 京 (jīng) is the sound hint, a rough match for jiù
尤 (yóu, outstanding) — the meaning-side part of the character

example.fact: 就 is a small adverb that links an earlier condition to a quick result: 一下课就回家 'go home as soon as class ends'. Compare 才 (cái), which suggests something happened later than expected: 他八点就到了 vs 他八点才到.

components.note: 人 (person) — the upper part; simplified from the traditional 會
云 (to say) — the lower part; in this simplified form it suggests people talking at a gathering

example.english: I can speak a little Chinese.
example.fact: 会 means 'can' for learned skills (会游泳 'can swim'), while 能 covers physical ability or permission. It also predicts the future: 明天会下雨 'it will probably rain'. The reading kuài shows up in 会计 'accountant'.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a spoken question particle
马 (mǎ) gives the sound, close to ma

example.fact: 吗 turns any statement into a yes/no question: 你有钱。→ 你有钱吗？ It stays toneless. Do not add 吗 to a question that already has a question word (什么, 谁, 哪儿); 你是谁吗 would be wrong.

components.note: 覀 (cover) — the upper part, standing in for the hands/waist frame
女 (woman) — the lower part; the character is usually explained as a woman with hands on her waist, 'waist' being the oldest meaning

example.english: I want a glass of water.
example.fact: 要 covers 'want', 'need' and 'will'; the negative of 'must' is 不用 or 别, not 不要 (which is 'don't want' or 'don't!'). It is the ancestor of the body-part character 腰 'waist', created by adding 月 'flesh'.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — indicates speaking
兑 (duì) is the sound part; the match is distant today

example.pinyin: Tā shuō Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.
example.fact: 说 also means 'to scold' (被老师说了) and, read shuì, 'to persuade' (游说). To repeat the verb with a degree complement, Chinese uses 说中文说得很好, as in the example.

components.note: 女 (woman) — marks the pronoun as female
也 (yě) — the same right-hand part as in 他, mainly a sound-alike

example.fact: 她 is a modern invention: the character became standard in the 1910s–20s, when writers wanted to translate European gendered pronouns. Before that, 他 covered both genders. Speech still has no he/she distinction, since both are tā.

components.note: 相 (xiāng) gives the sound, a close match for xiǎng
心 (heart) — thinking and feeling

example.fact: 想 is a softer 'want' than 要: 我想喝茶 'I'd like tea'. It also means 'to think about' (想一想) and 'to miss' (我想你). Do not use it for 'think that' in a belief about facts; 我觉得 is more usual.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke, the simplest picture of 'one'

example.fact: 一 changes tone: yí before a fourth tone (一个), yì before 1st–3rd tones (一杯). Alone, in counting or in a phone number it stays yī, and in phone numbers it is often said yāo to avoid confusion with 七 (qī).

components.note: 彳 (step) — a movement radical, an old link to the meaning
艮 (gèn) is the sound hint, a close match for hěn

example.fact: Before a one-word adjective, 很 is often just a bridge, not 'very': 她很高 simply means 'She is tall'. Without 很, 她高 sounds like a comparison. For real intensity, stress it or use 非常 or 特别.

components.note: A side view of a standing person, drawn with legs and an arm

example.fact: 人 is a base of countless words: 中国人 'Chinese person', 好人 'good person'. It takes no measure word of its own in 人们 'people', and in counting it uses 个 or the polite 位: 三个人 / 三位客人.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — spoken particle
巴 (bā) gives the sound, exactly as in this word's usual reading

example.fact: 吧 softens requests and suggestions: 走吧 'let's go', 你来吧 'come on'. At the end of a statement it signals a guess: 他是老师吧？ 'He's a teacher, right?' It is toneless in this use but bā in the noun 酒吧 'bar'.

components.note: 阝 (city/place) — the right-hand part; 那 began as a place name, with 'that' a borrowed sense

example.fact: Don't confuse 那 (nà, 'that') with 哪 (nǎ, 'which'): the second adds 口. 那 can also mean 'then, in that case' at the start of a reply: 那我们走吧 'Then let's go'. In speech it is often said nèi.

meanings: used before a verb to show intent

components.note: Originally a picture of a wheat plant (the character 麦 relates to it); 'come' was a borrowed use of the sound

example.fact: 来 is the speaker-oriented 'come' and pairs with 去 'go'. As a verb ending it shows direction toward the speaker: 拿来 'bring'. 来 also stands in for specific verbs in offers, such as 我来 'let me do it'.

components.note: 阝 (city) — the right-hand radical; the character's older reading dū means 'capital city'
者 (zhě) is the sound part; closer to the dū reading

example.fact: 都 'all' must come AFTER the thing it counts: 我们都去 (not 都我们去). It also means 'already': 都十二点了 'it's already twelve'. Read dū it means 'capital', as in 首都.

components.note: 人 (person) — the top part
丨 (vertical stroke) — a single mark; together they suggest one person or one item

example.fact: 个 is the all-purpose measure word, used when you don't know the specific one. It is toneless in speech (liǎng ge). It simplifies the traditional 個, and the same shape is also an old standalone character.

components.note: An ancient picture of a bear-like animal; the sense 'ability' is a borrowed meaning, and the animal sense survives in 熊

example.fact: 能 is 'can' by circumstance or ability: 我今天不能去 'I can't go today'. It differs from 会 (learned skill): 他会游泳, 但今天不能游 'he can swim, but can't today'. 能 also asks permission.

components.note: 土 (earth) — the upper part
厶 — the lower part; the modern parts are mainly shape, not a clear story

example.fact: 去 is movement away from the speaker, as 来 is toward. After a verb it marks direction away: 拿去 'take away'. A meaning 'last' appears in 去年 'last year'. Place words follow directly: 去北京, not 去到北京.

components.note: 氵 (water) — the original sense was 'to sink' in water
殳 (shū) is a distant sound hint

example.fact: 没 negates 有 and past events: 我没去 'I didn't go'. Don't combine it with 了 in that case. Written 没有 in full, with 有 often dropped in speech. In 没 mò ('to sink') it is a different, rarer reading.

components.note: 禾 (hé) gives the sound exactly
口 (mouth) — harmony of voices; the oldest meaning is 'in harmony'

example.pinyin: Wǒ hé péngyou qù kàn diànyǐng.
example.english: I'm going to see a movie with a friend.
example.fact: 和 joins nouns only: 苹果和香蕉 'apples and bananas'. To join verbs or sentences use 而且 or just a comma. In Taiwan 和 in this sense is often said hàn. It also forms 和平 'peace' and 和气 'friendly'.

components.note: 至 (arrive) — gives the meaning; it pictures something reaching a spot
刂 (dāo) gives the sound, a close match for dào

example.fact: 到 can follow another verb to show the result is reached: 找到 'find (successfully)', 看到 'catch sight of', 买到 'manage to buy'. As a preposition it means 'to': 从八点到九点 'from 8 to 9'.

components.note: 又 (hand) — one hand
寸 (hand) — another hand; the pair stands for two things facing each other; this is the simplified form of 對

example.fact: 对 is the quick 'right/correct' reply: 对！ 'Exactly!'. As a preposition it means 'towards' or 'about': 他对我很好 'He is nice to me'. 对不起 'sorry' literally means 'can't face (you)'.

components.note: Origin is uncertain; in modern use it is purely a grammar word, so treat the shape as a unit

example.fact: 也 goes before the verb, never at the end: 我也是学生. In negatives it means 'either': 我也不去. Pair 也 with 都 as 也都 in that order ('also all'), not 都也.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — spoken exclamation
阿 (ā) is the sound part, a direct match

example.fact: 啊 changes sound to blend with the previous word's ending: after -n it becomes na (难啊 nán na), after -i it becomes ya (是啊 shì ya), and it is sometimes written 呀 or 哇. It can express warmth, surprise or mild urging.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — motion; the verb sense 'to return' is the other reading huán
不 is part of the simplified shape, a shorthand rather than a meaning clue

example.fact: 还 has two readings: hái 'still, also' (还没吃 'haven't eaten yet') and huán 'to return': 还钱 'pay back money'. The adverb hái also compares: 比这个还好 'even better than this'.

meanings: marks the object before a verb
measure word for things with a handle

components.note: 扌 (hand) — grasping
巴 (bā) gives the sound, a near match for bǎ

example.fact: The 把 construction moves the object before the verb: 我把书放在桌子上 'I put the book on the table'. It focuses on what's done to the object, so the verb needs a result, e.g. 关上 or 放在. 把 is also a measure word for chairs and knives.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — asking or telling
上 stands in for the traditional sound part in 讓; here it's a shorthand

example.english: Mom told me to go to bed early.
example.fact: 让 means 'to let' or 'to have someone do': 让我看看 'let me see'. In a passive-like sentence it can mark the doer: 书让他拿走了 'the book was taken by him'. Its original meaning 'to yield' survives in 让座 'give up one's seat'.

components.note: 亻 (person) — a person acting
故 (gù) is only a loose sound hint

example.fact: 做 is the everyday 'do/make': 做饭 'cook', 做作业 'do homework'. It is a later variant of 作, which still appears in written compounds such as 工作 and 作者. 做 is preferred for hands-on tasks.

components.note: 纟 (silk thread) — an old link to 'supply, provide'
合 (hé) is a distant sound hint

example.pinyin: Wǒ gěi nǐ yì běn shū.
example.fact: 给 can be 'to give' (我给你) or a preposition 'for/to': 给我打电话 'call me'. After another verb it marks the recipient: 送给她 'give to her'. Read jǐ in compounds like 供给 'to supply'.

components.note: A short mark above a long line, a simple way to show 'above'

example.english: The book is on the table.
example.fact: 上 appears after a noun as 'on/above': 桌子上 'on the table'. It can mean 'previous': 上个月 'last month', and 上班 'go to work', 上学 'go to school'. Its opposite is 下.

components.note: 辶 (walk) — movement across
寸 replaces the traditional sound part in 過; it is a simplification, not a meaning clue

example.fact: After a verb, 过 shows experience: 我吃过 'I've eaten it before'. As a full verb it means 'to pass/spend': 过年 'celebrate the New Year', 过马路 'cross the road'. In the experience use it is toneless.

meanings: particle linking a verb to its result or degree

components.note: 彳 (step) — going to get something
寸 (hand) — a hand holding the prize; the extra right-hand part is a simplified shape

example.fact: 得 (de) links a verb to how well or how far it goes: 说得好 'speaks well'. The same character is dé in the sense 'to obtain' (得到) and děi 'must' (我得走). Each reading does a different job.

components.note: 手 (hand) — held above the eye
目 (eye) — what is doing the looking

example.fact: 看 pictures a hand shading the eye. It covers 'look', 'watch' and 'read': 看书, 看电视. As a softener it means 'try': 尝尝看 'give it a taste'. Read kān it means 'to guard', as in 看守.

components.note: 直 (straight) — one part of the modern form
几 (small table) — the base; the pieces are best treated as a memory aid, not the true origin

example.fact: 真 is the common 'really' in exclamations: 真好 'how nice'. As an adjective it means 'real': 真的 'true'. 真的吗？ is a standard 'Really?' and 真不错 is a modest compliment.

components.note: 羊 (sheep) — the upper part, a visual element of the form
目 (eye) — the lower part; together they are a memory aid for this form, not its true origin

example.fact: 着 after a verb gives a lasting state: 坐着 'sitting', 穿着 'wearing'. It is neutral on the action itself. Other readings include zháo ('to catch on', 睡着 'fall asleep') and zhuó in written words like 着手.

components.note: The old form shows a hand holding a tool, related to 史; the sense is 'handling affairs'

example.fact: 事 covers 'affair, matter': 有事 'be busy', 没事 'it's nothing / no problem', 出事 'have an accident'. It is a frequent word for abstract matters, while 东西 means physical 'things'.

components.note: 占 (zhān) gives a distant sound hint
灬 (fire dots) — the dots at the bottom suggest the traditional 點 'dot'

example.fact: 点 gives the hour: 三点 'three o'clock'. 一点 means 'a little' (说慢一点 'speak a bit slower'). It also means 'to order' dishes (点菜) and 'to tick, to nod' (点头).

components.note: 口 (mouth) — a spoken particle
尼 (ní) is the sound part, a near match

example.fact: 呢 makes a follow-up question that reuses the topic: 你呢？ 'And you?'. 我的书呢？ means 'Where's my book?'. It can also mark that something is going on: 他在睡觉呢. It is toneless.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — the upper part
八 (eight, 'divide') — the lower part, like words flowing from the mouth

example.english: I can only speak a tiny bit.
example.fact: This 只 (zhǐ) is 'only'; the same-looking 隻 simplified to 只 is the measure word zhī for animals (一只猫). 只有 means 'only if' and 只要 means 'as long as'.

components.note: 另 (lìng, 'separate') — the left part
刂 (knife) — cutting apart, to separate

example.english: Don't forget to bring an umbrella.
example.fact: 别 before a verb gives a command: 别走 'don't go'. It is a shortened form of 不要. The noun sense 'other' appears in 别人 'other people', and the sense 'to part' in 告别 'say goodbye'.
